title: Cache Invalidation & Stampedes
subtitle: Watch a hot cache entry expire under load, see the database get flattened, then apply the fixes one by one.
learn: How TTL expiry and explicit invalidation each trade freshness against complexity
Why a delete-then-refill race can leave stale data in the cache
What a cache stampede (thundering herd) is and why it hurts the database most
How request coalescing and probabilistic early expiry prevent stampedes
Why a single hot key can overload one cache node, and how to spread it

steps.title: A cache that works too well
steps.body: A shop's home page shows a product feed that takes the database about 200 ms to build. The site gets 5,000 reads per second, and 99.9% of them are cache hits, so the database sees only about 5 queries per second. The feed is one hot key (a cache entry everybody asks for), rebuilt about once a minute. Everything looks calm. The questions: how does old data ever get replaced, and what happens when this one entry suddenly disappears?
steps.idea: A cache hides load from the database, so anything that empties it can expose that load all at once.
steps.caption: Healthy: nearly every read is answered by the cache.

steps.title: TTL: let it expire
steps.body: The simplest way to refresh a cache is a TTL (time to live): a countdown stored with the entry. Here the app saves the feed with a 60 second TTL, and the cache silently drops it when time is up. The next reader gets a miss, rebuilds the feed from the database (about 200 ms for that one request), and saves it again. No services need to coordinate, which is why TTL is the default. The cost: data can be up to 60 seconds old.
steps.idea: TTL is the cheapest invalidation: no coordination, but a built-in staleness window.
steps.caption: A miss rebuilds the entry from the database, about 200 ms for that one request.

steps.title: Stale reads
steps.body: Now an admin changes a price in the database. The cache does not know, so it keeps serving the old feed until the TTL runs out. For up to that long, every shopper sees the old price. For a news feed that is fine. For a price, stock count, or permission it can mean selling at the wrong price or showing access a user should no longer have. A shorter TTL reduces staleness, but entries are rebuilt more often, so the database does more work.
steps.idea: Staleness is bounded by the TTL; a shorter TTL buys freshness with more database work.
steps.caption: The database has the new price, but the cache still returns the old one.

steps.title: Explicit invalidation
steps.body: To avoid waiting, the writer deletes the cache key right after the database change commits (is saved for good). The next read misses and loads the new value. Deleting is usually better than overwriting the cache, because a delete is idempotent (safe to repeat) and never writes a value that could arrive out of order. It is not airtight: a reader that loaded the old row just before the commit can write it into the cache just after the delete. So teams keep a TTL as a safety net even when they also invalidate.
steps.idea: Invalidate by deleting after the write commits, and keep a TTL to repair the races you missed.
steps.caption: The writer saves to the database first, then deletes the cache key.

steps.title: The stampede
steps.body: Now the key disappears, by TTL or by a delete, while 5,000 requests per second arrive. Every request misses and starts its own 200 ms query. During the first rebuild, about 5,000 x 0.2 = 1,000 identical queries are sent. If the database comfortably handles about 500 queries per second, it queues, slows down, and requests time out. Failed rebuilds leave the key empty, so the pile-on continues. This is a cache stampede, also called a thundering herd.
steps.idea: A stampede turns one expired key into thousands of identical database queries, and the overload can prevent the refill that would end it.
steps.caption: Every request misses and sends its own query to the database.

steps.title: Request coalescing
steps.body: The fix: let only one request rebuild. The first request to miss takes a short lock (in one process, a single-flight map; across servers, a cache entry created only if absent, with a short expiry). Only that request queries the database. Others wait for its result, or briefly serve the previous value if you kept one. The database sees one query instead of a thousand, and waiters pay at most one rebuild time (about 200 ms). Give the lock its own timeout so a crashed leader cannot block the key forever.
steps.idea: Coalescing collapses many identical misses into one rebuild; always give the lock an expiry.
steps.caption: One request rebuilds the entry; the others wait up to about 200 ms.

steps.title: Refresh before it expires
steps.body: Coalescing still makes some people wait. Probabilistic early expiry avoids even that. Each request that reads the entry may randomly decide to rebuild it early. The chance rises as expiry gets closer, and rises with how long a rebuild takes. One lucky request refreshes the entry while everyone else keeps getting the still-valid value. The entry is usually replaced before it expires, so a mass miss becomes very unlikely. Stale-while-revalidate, which serves the old value during a refresh, is a close cousin.
steps.idea: Rebuilding slightly early, at random, means the key is never empty when the crowd arrives.
steps.caption: One request refreshes early in the background; the rest still hit.

steps.title: Many keys, one deadline
steps.body: A related trap: a warm-up job or bulk load writes 100,000 keys, all with a 60 second TTL. They all expire together, so the database faces a stampede across many different keys at once. Suppose 40 percent of requests (2,000 of 5,000 per second) land on keys that just expired. Coalescing works per key, so it cannot shrink 100,000 distinct queries. The cheap fix is jitter: add a random amount, say plus or minus 10 percent, to each TTL so expiries spread out. Make the window wide enough that rebuilds stay under what the database can handle.
steps.idea: Add random jitter to TTLs so keys written together do not expire together.
steps.caption: Keys that expire in the same second overwhelm the database.

steps.title: Hot keys
steps.body: Even with no misses, one key can be the problem. Suppose a celebrity's profile is read 150,000 times per second. That key lives on one cache node, and a single node serves roughly 100,000 simple operations per second (a rule of thumb; large values hit network limits sooner). That node is overloaded while other nodes sit idle. Fixes: a tiny in-process cache on each app server with a 1 to 5 second TTL, or several copies under keys like profile#1 to profile#8, read at random so reads spread out. The cost: a write must delete every copy, and a local cache can be stale for its TTL.
steps.idea: Hot keys are a load-spreading problem: copy the value so reads fan out across nodes.
steps.caption: Reads are spread over copies of the hot key (profile#1 to #8).

steps.title: Keep the herd away
steps.body: TTL is simple but leaves a window of stale data. Deleting the key on write shrinks that window, with a TTL kept as a backstop. An empty hot key sends every request to the database at once, so coalesce rebuilds, refresh early at random, and add jitter to TTLs. For hot keys, copy the value across nodes or cache it locally for a second or two. Measure miss bursts, not just the average hit rate.
steps.idea: Plan for the moment the cache is empty, not only for the moment it is full.
steps.caption: Healthy again: few DB queries, high hit rate.

quiz.q: A key with a 60 s TTL is read 2,000 times per second and takes 500 ms to rebuild. It expires with no protection. Roughly how many database queries fire for it before the first rebuild finishes?
quiz.why: Every request that arrives during the 500 ms rebuild also misses: 2,000 req/s x 0.5 s = about 1,000 duplicate queries.

quiz.q: Why do many systems delete the cache key after a write instead of writing the new value into the cache?
options: Deleting is faster than any write
A delete is idempotent and never writes a possibly out-of-order value; the next read loads fresh data
It removes the need for a TTL
quiz.why: Setting a value from the writer can race with other writers and store an out-of-order result. A delete is safe to repeat, and the next reader rebuilds from the source of truth. It does not remove every race, which is why a TTL stays as a backstop.

quiz.q: Which change best protects against 100,000 different keys all expiring in the same second after a bulk load?
options: Adding random jitter to each TTL
quiz.why: Per-key coalescing cannot merge queries for different keys. Jitter spreads the expiry times so the rebuild work is spread out over time.

quiz.q: One key receives 150,000 reads per second, more than one cache node can serve, and the node is saturated, though the hit rate is 99.99%. What is the right fix?
options: Spread reads over copies of the key or add a short-lived in-process cache
Raise the TTL so it expires less often
quiz.why: This is a hot key problem, not a miss problem: 150,000 reads per second exceeds the roughly 100,000 operations per second one node can handle. The load is concentrated on one node, so you copy the value to spread reads across nodes or keep it in each app server's memory for a second or two.

cheatsheet.def: Time to live: how long a cached entry may be served before it is dropped. Bounds staleness without any coordination.
Writers delete (or update) the cache key when the source data changes. Fresher than TTL but needs every write path to remember to do it.
Many requests miss the same key at once and all hit the database to rebuild it. Also called a thundering herd or dogpile.
Only one request rebuilds a missing key; others wait or use the old value. Also called single-flight. Give the lock a timeout.
Each reader may refresh early with a rising probability near expiry, so the key is replaced before it expires.
Serve the old value while one background request fetches a new one. Trades a little staleness for no waiting.
Add a random offset, such as plus or minus 10 percent, to TTLs so keys written together do not expire together.
A single key with far more traffic than others. It can saturate one cache node. Fix by replicating it or caching locally with a short TTL.
